title: Principles of prevention & Delivering Better Oral Health
blurb: Why prevention beats repair, the three levels of prevention, and how the UK's Delivering Better Oral Health toolkit guides every patient's advice.
question: A new patient tells you they only come to the dentist when something hurts, and asks why the practice keeps talking about brushing and sugar. The dentist asks you to explain the practice's preventive approach. What guidance is it based on, and what would every patient be told?

teach.body: Most oral disease is largely preventable: dental caries, gum disease, tooth wear and much oral cancer all have known causes such as plaque, sugar, acids, tobacco and alcohol. A filling repairs the damage but does nothing about the cause, so new decay keeps coming. Prevention tackles the cause. It means less pain, less treatment, lower cost and healthier mouths for life, which is why it sits at the heart of modern UK dentistry.

steps.label: Primary
steps.sub: Stop disease starting: fluoride toothpaste, diet advice, fissure sealants

steps.label: Secondary
steps.sub: Catch it early and halt it: spot a white spot lesion, apply varnish, improve brushing

steps.label: Tertiary
steps.sub: Limit the damage of established disease: fillings, root canal treatment, dentures

teach.caption: The earlier you act, the less treatment the patient needs. Most of a dental nurse's preventive work is primary and secondary.

teach.body: DBOH is the UK's evidence-based toolkit for prevention, now in its 4th edition (last updated September 2025). It is issued jointly by the Department of Health and Social Care, NHS England, the Welsh Government and the Department of Health Northern Ireland, with support from the four UK Chief Dental Officers. In Scotland it informs oral health policy. Its summary tables tell the dental team exactly what advice and treatment to give for caries, periodontal disease, oral cancer and tooth wear.

head: Grade
What it means
Example
rows: High confidence the benefits outweigh harms
Varnish twice a year for all 3–6s
Daily fluoride rinse if at higher risk
teach.caption: Conditional does not mean 'doesn't work'. It means the evidence is less certain.

teach.h: Advice for everyone, extra for patients giving concern
teach.body: DBOH says every patient should get preventive advice and support, not just those thought to be at risk. On top of that, 'patients giving concern' get extra measures. These include people with current or past decay, children whose brothers or sisters have had decay, people with physical or learning disabilities, medically compromised patients (for example with diabetes), frail older people, people on medicines that cause dry mouth, people who are homeless and people facing social disadvantage. Risk is reassessed at every recall, because it changes across life.

teach.h: Risk decides the level of support

children.label: Core advice for all
children.sub: Recall up to 12 months (child) or 24 months (adult)

children.label: Core advice + extra
children.sub: Stronger fluoride, more varnish, diet review, shorter recall

teach.caption: DBOH recall ranges: children 3–12 months, adults 3–24 months, set by the dentist according to need and risk.

head: Message
Protects against
rows: Brush twice daily: last thing at night + one other time
Cut the amount and how often you have sugar
Don't use tobacco; keep alcohol within 14 units a week

teach.h: Your part as a dental nurse
teach.body: Under the GDC Scope of Practice, giving oral health advice and education is part of your role, and with extra training you can apply fluoride varnish on a dentist's prescription. You do not diagnose or decide treatment. Use every contact to reinforce the key messages (the NHS calls this Making Every Contact Count), tailor advice to the patient in front of you, and record the advice given in the notes. Advice should always follow the evidence, which is what DBOH provides.

teach.text: Prevention is not just for children or 'high-risk' patients. DBOH is clear that ALL patients should receive preventive advice; patients giving concern get additional measures on top.

items: Primary = stop it starting; secondary = catch it early and halt it; tertiary = limit the damage.
DBOH (4th edn) is the UK evidence-based prevention toolkit, covering caries, gum disease, oral cancer and tooth wear.
Advice is graded strong, conditional or good practice.
Everyone gets core advice; patients giving concern get extra. Risk is reassessed at every recall.
Nurses give advice within scope and record it; they don't diagnose or plan treatment.

summary: You can now explain why prevention matters, sort preventive measures into primary, secondary and tertiary, describe what Delivering Better Oral Health is and how it grades advice, identify patients giving concern, and give the core messages every patient should hear within your scope as a dental nurse.

A.q: Which publication is the main evidence-based prevention toolkit used by dental teams across the UK?
options: The Ottawa Charter for Health Promotion
A.why: Delivering Better Oral Health (4th edition) is the UK's evidence-based toolkit for preventing oral disease.

whyNot.0: The Eatwell Guide is general healthy-eating guidance; DBOH refers to it but it is not the prevention toolkit.
whyNot.1: HTM 01-05 covers decontamination in dental practices, not oral disease prevention.
whyNot.3: The Ottawa Charter is an international health promotion framework, not a dental clinical toolkit.

A.q: The dentist spots an early white spot lesion and asks you to prepare fluoride varnish to help it remineralise. Which level of prevention is this?
A.why: Detecting disease early and halting or reversing it before a cavity forms is secondary prevention.

whyNot.0: Primary prevention stops disease starting at all; here the lesion already exists.
whyNot.2: Tertiary prevention limits damage from established disease, such as restoring a cavity.
whyNot.3: Population prevention describes community-wide measures, not care for one patient's lesion.

A.q: Which patient does DBOH describe as a 'patient giving concern' for caries?
options: An adult with no decay for ten years
A teenager who brushes twice a day
A child whose sister has had decay
An adult who attends every six months
A.why: DBOH lists children whose siblings have caries experience among those giving concern.

whyNot.0: Years without decay suggest lower risk, not higher.
whyNot.1: Brushing twice daily is a protective habit, not a risk factor.
whyNot.3: Regular attendance on its own doesn't make a patient higher risk.

B.q: A DBOH recommendation is graded 'good practice'. What does this mean?
options: It is backed by high-certainty trials
It is optional and rarely useful
It is based on expert consensus
B.why: Good practice points rest on clinical consensus and expert opinion where no robust research exists.

whyNot.0: High-certainty evidence usually supports a 'strong' recommendation.
whyNot.1: Good practice advice is well established and should still be followed.
whyNot.2: Good practice points appear across all age groups in DBOH.

B.q: A patient has a large cavity restored and a crown fitted. Which level of prevention does this represent?
B.why: Restoring established disease to limit further damage and keep the tooth working is tertiary prevention.

whyNot.1: Secondary prevention would have caught the lesion before it became a cavity.
whyNot.2: Primary prevention stops disease from starting.
whyNot.3: Health promotion enables people to improve their health; it is not a restoration.

B.q: According to DBOH, what recall interval range can the dentist set for an adult?
options: Once a year for all adults
B.why: DBOH gives adults a recall range of 3 to 24 months, set according to oral health needs and disease risk.

whyNot.0: A fixed six-monthly recall for everyone is not evidence-based; intervals depend on risk.
whyNot.1: A fixed yearly recall ignores individual risk.
whyNot.3: Waiting for symptoms means disease is already established; prevention needs regular review.

C.q: Which of these tasks is within a dental nurse's scope of practice?
C.why: Oral health advice and education are part of every dental nurse's role under the GDC Scope of Practice.

whyNot.0: Dental nurses do not diagnose disease.
whyNot.2: Setting the recall interval is a clinical decision made by the dentist.
whyNot.3: Prescribing is done by the dentist, not the dental nurse.

C.q: How often does DBOH say a patient's risk of oral disease should be reassessed?
C.why: Risk changes across life, so DBOH says it should be assessed at every dental recall visit.

whyNot.0: Risk changes over time, so a single assessment soon goes out of date.
whyNot.1: Five years is far too long; risk can change much faster.
whyNot.2: Waiting for new decay means prevention has already failed.

C.q: Which statement about Delivering Better Oral Health is correct?
options: It gives advice for every patient
It is written for children's teeth only
It is used only in England
C.why: DBOH says all patients should receive preventive advice, with extra measures for those giving concern.

whyNot.1: It also covers periodontal disease, oral cancer and tooth wear.
whyNot.2: It has tables for adults as well as children.
whyNot.3: It is issued jointly for England, Wales and Northern Ireland, and informs policy in Scotland.

reteach.title: Think of it like looking after a car
reteach.question: A car gets regular oil changes, a warning light tells you something's wrong, and a garage repairs breakdowns. How does that match the three levels of prevention?

blocks.body: Regular servicing stops problems starting: that's primary prevention, like brushing with fluoride toothpaste and cutting sugar. A warning light lets you fix a small fault before it becomes a breakdown: that's secondary prevention, like spotting a white spot lesion and applying varnish. A repair after a breakdown gets the car running again but it is never quite as good as new: that's tertiary prevention, like a filling or crown. DBOH is the service manual.

blocks.text: If the disease is already there but caught early and stopped, it's secondary. If it has caused damage that needs repairing, it's tertiary.

explain.body: Primary prevention stops disease starting. Secondary prevention detects it early and halts or reverses it. Tertiary prevention limits the damage once disease is established and restores function.

steps.label: Primary
steps.sub: Healthy tooth: keep it that way

test.q: Placing a fissure sealant on a healthy, newly erupted molar is which level of prevention?
test.why: The tooth is healthy and the sealant stops decay starting, so this is primary prevention.

whyNot.0: Secondary prevention acts on disease that has already begun.
whyNot.3: Palliative care relieves symptoms; it doesn't prevent disease.

explain.body: Delivering Better Oral Health, 4th edition, is the UK's evidence-based prevention toolkit. Its tables set out advice for all patients and extra measures for those giving concern, graded strong, conditional or good practice.

items.label: diseases: caries, gum disease, oral cancer, tooth wear

test.q: Which four conditions do the DBOH summary tables cover?
options: Caries, gum disease, oral cancer, tooth wear
Caries, mouth ulcers, oral thrush, dry socket
Gum disease, TMJ pain, cold sores, caries
test.why: The DBOH summary tables cover prevention of dental caries, periodontal diseases, oral cancer and tooth wear.

whyNot.1: Ulcers, thrush and dry socket are not the subject of DBOH's summary tables.
whyNot.2: TMJ pain and cold sores aren't covered by the tables.
whyNot.3: Fluorosis, abscess and halitosis are not among the four table topics.

explain.body: These are people at higher risk, or for whom disease or its treatment would be especially difficult. Examples: current or past decay, siblings with decay, disabilities, medical conditions such as diabetes, frailty, dry-mouth medicines, homelessness and social disadvantage.

rows.label: Child whose brother needed extractions under GA
Patient on medication causing dry mouth
Adult with no decay history, brushing well

test.q: Which patient would DBOH class as giving concern?
options: A teenager with no decay history
A child who uses a smear of paste
An older person who is frail
test.why: Mentally and physically frail older people are listed by DBOH as patients giving concern.

whyNot.0: No decay history suggests lower risk.
whyNot.2: A smear of toothpaste is the correct advice for under-3s, not a risk factor.

explain.body: Everyone hears the same core messages: brush twice daily with fluoride toothpaste, spit don't rinse, cut sugar, clean between teeth, avoid tobacco and limit alcohol. You give this advice within your scope and record it.

letters.sub: Last thing at night + one other time

test.q: When does DBOH advise one of the two daily toothbrushing sessions should happen?
test.why: DBOH advises brushing last thing at night (or before bedtime) and on at least one other occasion.

whyNot.0: Lunchtime isn't specified; night-time brushing is the key session.
whyNot.2: Morning brushing is fine as the second session, but night-time is the one DBOH names.
whyNot.3: Brushing after every snack isn't the advice; cutting snack frequency is.
